query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an aluminizing coating to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will form a protective Al2O3-rich oxide scale during high-temperature exposure, preventing pesting and improving oxygen resistance while preserving room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with BCC crystal structure, exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but suffering from severe oxidation (pestering) in air.
generation.intervention: Aluminizing (surface coating with aluminum) to form an Al-rich layer that oxidizes to Al2O3.

conditions.loading: Unloaded during oxidation; mechanical properties tested post-exposure

generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 oxide scale that acts as a diffusion barrier against oxygen ingress, preventing internal oxidation and pesting.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum in the coating preferentially oxidizes to form a dense, thermodynamically stable Al2O3 layer with low oxygen permeability, inhibiting the rapid internal oxidation and catastrophic disintegration (pestering) observed in uncoated HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.predicted_outcome: Significantly reduced mass gain (e.g., <10 mg/cm² after 100 h at 800 °C vs. >55 mg/cm² for uncoated), no pesting, and retention of >80% of original room- and high-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength.
generation.baseline: Uncoated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibits severe pesting and mass gain of ~55 mg/cm² after 100 h at 700 °C in air, with complete structural degradation.
generation.boundary: Intervention effective up to 1000 °C; mechanical property degradation expected if coating spalls or if Al content exceeds solubility limits causing brittle intermetallic formation in the bulk.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty exists regarding long-term coating adhesion at >900 °C and potential embrittlement if Al diffuses into the bulk alloy forming brittle phases; exact ductility retention depends on coating thickness and processing method.
generation.falsification_experiment: Expose uncoated and aluminized equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr samples to air at 800 °C for 100 hours. If the aluminized sample exhibits mass gain >30 mg/cm² or shows visible pesting (crumbling/disintegration), the hypothesis is falsified. Additionally, if post-oxidation tensile tests show ductility <5% at room temperature, the intervention fails the mechanical preservation constraint.

As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. By combining refractory elements such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, Hf, …etc. in equi- or near equi-molar ratios, several RHEAs with promising mechanical properties have been reported [5] – [7] . However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties.
